comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s1, s2) describe the three-year curriculum in words only: a common first year with two semester-long group projects, a second year with core courses and one module per semester chosen from two (Intelligent Interaction or AI & Machine Learning in semester 3; High Performance Computing or Cybersecurity in semester 4), and a flexible third year in which semester 5 offers elective courses with a Brightlands Campus Project, a minor or a semester abroad and semester 6 combines the last core courses with the bachelor's thesis. They give no course list or EC. The course-level reconstruction therefore uses the Faculty of Science and Engineering CS course catalogue (s3), the most recent course-level publication reachable from this environment (academic year 2025-2026; curriculum.maastrichtuniversity.nl, which holds the 2026-2027 courses, was unreachable), which gives 4 EC to every period course, 6 EC to the semester projects, 10 EC to each module, 18 EC to the bachelor's thesis and the 30 EC semester options; the programme pages describe the same structure for the current year. Year 1 totals 60 EC (12 courses of 4 EC and two projects of 6 EC), year 2 totals 60 EC (ten courses of 4 EC and two 10-EC modules), and year 3 totals 60 EC: Project 3-1 (6 EC), six elective courses (24 EC, derived by arithmetic as 30 EC less the project; the catalogue says third-year students choose three electives in each of periods 1 and 2 from the optional courses, and the page adds courses from the Faculty of Science and Engineering, so the space is preserved as one open elective component), three core courses in period 4 (12 EC) and the 18-EC thesis. The catalogue lists two Operating Systems courses with identical descriptions (BCS2140 in year 2 and BCS3420 in year 3, period 4); both are counted as listed, and a human may want to confirm the year-3 listing against the current Education and Examination Regulations. The honours tracks (CS@Work, MaRBLe 2.0), the minor, the educational minor and the semester abroad are alternatives to the elective option and are not part of the reconstructed pathway.

routeSelection.route: Year 2 modules Intelligent Interaction (semester 3) and High Performance Computing (semester 4); year 3 semester 1 elective courses with Project 3-1
routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Computer Science bachelor, so no named route applies, but the official curriculum requires one module in each of semesters 3 and 4 and offers three options in year 3 semester 5, and these choices must be instantiated to obtain one 180-EC pathway. The two modules of each semester (Intelligent Interaction and AI & Machine Learning; High Performance Computing and Cybersecurity) are equally central to the programme, which states that students specialise in two of four topics, and no module is evidently more representative of the broad identity of computer science, so the first-listed module of each semester in the official curriculum is used as the neutral tie-break. For semester 5 the elective courses with the Brightlands Campus Project keep the pathway within computer science, whereas the minor and the semester abroad are explicitly meant to move outside the main field or institution.

core: Programming and software construction: procedural and object-oriented programming, software engineering and architectures, programming languages and the building of complete software products in project work
Algorithms and computation: data structures and algorithms, algorithmic design and the theory of computing, with algorithmic and computational thinking
Mathematical and logical foundations: discrete mathematics, logic, calculus, linear algebra, statistics and numerical methods
Computer systems: computer architecture, operating systems, computer networks, databases and parallel programming
Research and project practice: project-centred learning in every semester and a bachelor's thesis carried out as an independent research project with a research plan
adjacent: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, the AI and Machine Learning module, intelligent agents and learning from data

Intelligent interaction and robotics: human-computer interaction, Intelligent User Interfaces, image and video processing and robotics, with a laboratory for cognitive robotics and complex intelligent systems

Computing in society and technology enterprise: the history and philosophy of computing, including whether machines can think and whether ethics can be designed into computer systems, and the Startup Engineering elective and the start-up route named in the programme's own material
Specialised systems directions: high-performance computing, cybersecurity, embedded systems and quantum computing, together with the signals, control and numerical mathematics they rely on
Teaching computer science: an educational minor preparing students to teach computer science
questions: How can machines act intelligently, perceive their environment and interact with people?
How can reliable, complete software systems be designed and built in teams for real clients and for critical sectors such as healthcare and energy?
What can be computed at all, and how efficiently can it be computed?

alternatives.label: Computer Science with Mathematics, Data and Artificial Intelligence
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has six courses on programming, software development, algorithms, databases and networks and operating systems (introductory programming, software development, algorithms and data structures, advanced algorithms, database management and networks and operating systems), seven on mathematics and logic (Mathematical Methods, logic and discrete mathematics, linear algebra, numerical methods, advanced calculus, linear systems, probability and statistics), six on data science, machine learning, computer vision and AI (introduction to data science, machine learning, deep learning, image processing, decision-making in AI and optimisation in AI), four on AI ethics, research methods, entrepreneurship and digital strategy, and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a computer-science programme with strong mathematical and data/AI strands, but UCR has no computer-architecture, security, parallel-computing, embedded-systems or theory-of-computing course, so the label names computer science with these strands and does not present it as a full computer-science degree.
alternatives.concept: UM's Computer Science bachelor is organised around programming and software engineering, algorithms, mathematical and logical foundations, computer systems (architecture, operating systems, networks, databases), project-centred and research practice, and a choice of specialist modules such as intelligent interaction and AI and machine learning. The strongest defensible UCR response reproduces the core that UCR can teach: programming, software development, algorithms and data structures, databases, networks and operating systems, a full mathematical track in calculus, linear algebra, discrete mathematics, numerical methods and probability and statistics, and a strand on data science, machine learning, deep learning, computer vision and AI planning and search that mirrors UM's artificial-intelligence and intelligent-interaction content. Computer architecture, security, parallel programming, embedded programming, programming languages and the theory of computing are not offered at UCR and stay unmatched; research methods and entrepreneurship stand in for the research and start-up practice around UM's projects and thesis.
progression: Introduction to Programming and Logic & Discrete Mathematics open semester 1 and precede every dependent course; Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics, Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Advanced Calculus and Neural Networks & Deep Learning; Algorithms & Data Structures and Networks & Operating Systems (semester 3) precede Advanced Algorithms and Software Development (semester 4); Machine Learning, Decision-making in AI and Probability & Statistics (semester 5) precede Neural Networks & Deep Learning and Optimization Methods in AI (semester 6); Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations (semester 5) precedes Strategy & Digital Transformation (semester 6).

alternatives.label: Artificial Intelligence and Intelligent Systems: Machine Learning, Robotics, Cognition and Ethics
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has eight courses on data science, machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, computer vision, robotics, AI planning and AI optimisation, eight on programming, algorithms, logic and the mathematics of learning and control (introductory programming, algorithms and data structures, logic and discrete mathematics, Mathematical Methods, linear algebra, numerical methods, linear systems and probability and statistics), four on brain, perception, cognition and research statistics (the brain and behaviour gateway, perception and action, higher order functions, statistics and experimental methods), three on philosophy of mind, ethics and AI ethics, and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a programme on artificial intelligence and intelligent systems with their cognitive and ethical context, not a general computer-science programme, because it has no course on databases, networks and operating systems, software engineering or advanced algorithms.
alternatives.concept: UM's Computer Science programme lets students specialise in Intelligent Interaction or AI and Machine Learning, and its material names intelligent systems and cognitive robotics, human-computer interaction and a laboratory for cognitive robotics and complex intelligent systems among the programme's applications. This alternative takes that direction as its organising logic instead of the broad computer-science core of Alternative 1: machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, decision-making and optimisation in AI, computer vision and robotics, supported by the mathematics of learning and control, with brain, perception and cognition and the philosophy and ethics of intelligent machines as the human side of intelligent systems and interaction. The software-engineering, systems, database, advanced-algorithm and business courses of Alternative 1 are replaced by this AI, cognition and philosophy strand.
progression: Introduction to Programming, the brain and behaviour gateway and Introduction to Data Science open semester 1; Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Linear Algebra, Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Robotics and Neural Networks & Deep Learning; Machine Learning and Linear Algebra (semester 3) precede Neural Networks & Deep Learning and Reinforcement Learning in the final semester; Statistics & Experimental Methods (semester 3) precedes Higher Order Functions (semester 5); Perception & Action (semester 4) follows the brain and behaviour gateway; Algorithms & Data Structures and Decision-making in AI (semester 5) precede Optimization Methods in AI and Reinforcement Learning (semester 6).
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 reproduces UM's broad computer-science core and has only a few AI courses; Alternative 2 takes the artificial-intelligence and intelligent-interaction direction as its organising logic. It keeps sixteen courses from Alternative 1 (the programming, mathematics, data-science and AI spine, including Personal & Professional Development) and replaces eight of them (Networks & Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, Software Development, Advanced Algorithms, Advanced Calculus, Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Research Methods & Statistics and Strategy & Digital Transformation) with reinforcement learning, robotics, the brain and behaviour gateway, perception and action, higher order functions, statistics and experimental methods, philosophy of mind and ethics. The two programmes differ by 8 courses (60 EC), above the 30 EC / 4-course floor, and the differing courses follow from the change of organising logic: they trade software engineering, systems and business for cognitive science and philosophy and for deeper AI methods, which Alternative 1 treats only through its shared AI courses.

selection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible. Alternative 1 owns the nine generator-eligible rows that describe the computer-science core (6184 computer science, 6185 software engineering, 6186 programming, 6187 how computers work, 6188 algorithms, 6189 logic and mathematics, 6195 computer networks, 6200 complete software products and 6201 computer-science research). Alternative 2 follows the artificial-intelligence and intelligent-interaction direction (6190 AI and machine learning, 6191 human-computer interaction, 6197 intelligent systems and robotics) and shares 16 courses with Alternative 1, so each programme differs from the other by 8 courses (60 EC) and the pair passes the 30 EC / 4-course floor. A third alternative was tested against the remaining generator-eligible rows and none could be implemented as a valid 24-course UCR programme: cybersecurity (6193, 6194), high-performance and parallel computing (6192), embedded systems (6196), quantum computing (6198) and teaching computer science (6202) each rest on courses UCR does not offer (UCR has no security, parallel-computing, computer-architecture, embedded-systems, physics or education course and only one networks and operating-systems course, already in Alternative 1), so they were rejected as not-feasible; software for organisations and critical sectors applied with business partners (6199, 6203) would be built from the same software-development, database and data courses as Alternative 1 and generic business additions that the target's evidence does not specify, so it was rejected as not-substantively-distinct. There are no support-only rows, and the search-only rows (6204 to 6213) generated no alternative; no row is inherited across split targets.

blocks: Both teach the basics of programming with data types, branching, loops and functions and with debugging and testing; Introduction to Programming is taught in Python and also covers object-oriented constructs, which UM teaches separately in Objects in Programming, and does not reproduce UM's introduction to computer organisation.

Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course gives UM's survey of computer-science concepts that combines algorithms, computer architecture, models of computation, networks and operating systems with a microcontroller laboratory.

Explicitly unmatched: the object-oriented constructs of Objects in Programming (classes, interfaces, polymorphism, event handling and graphical interfaces in Java) are only touched by one part of Introduction to Programming, which is already placed against Procedural Programming.

Both address the software development process: requirements, design, testing and quality assurance, and maintenance; Software Development adds programming in C++ and Haskell with code reviews and does not cover UM's software architectural design and architectures.

Explicitly unmatched: Software Development teaches two languages but not the analytical toolkit for understanding, interpreting and compiling programming languages of Principles of Programming Languages.
Algorithms, logic and the theory of computing

Both teach the design and analysis of algorithms together with data structures and their performance; the UCR course is built around laboratory work and experimental performance analysis, while UM's course treats lists, trees, graphs and strings with recursion, divide-and-conquer and dynamic programming.

Both extend the first algorithms course with advanced algorithm design and analysis; Advanced Algorithms covers algebraic algorithms and optimisation methods with mathematical modelling, whereas Algorithmic Design covers greedy methods, dynamic programming, recursive analysis and the justification of intractability, so the relationship is partial.

Both build a mathematical framework of logic and discrete structures for computer science; Logic & Discrete Mathematics applies them to algorithm construction, while UM's course concentrates on proof techniques.

Explicitly unmatched: the only UCR logic content sits in Logic & Discrete Mathematics, already placed against Discrete Mathematics, and UCR has no course on propositional and first-order logic systems, semantic tableaux, natural deduction or Hoare logic.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on models of computation, computability or complexity classes.

Both teach differential and integral calculus with problem solving; Mathematical Methods adds complex numbers and differential equations and applies the techniques in projects, whereas Calculus also treats limits, sequences and series.
Both teach systems of linear equations, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.
Both teach probability theory, distributions and statistical inference; Probability & Statistics adds parameter estimation and simulation with computer algebra.

Both teach numerical methods for root finding, differentiation and differential equations with attention to algorithm accuracy; UM's course adds floating-point representation and iterative methods for linear systems.

Both teach the layered architecture of computer networks with the Internet and its protocols as the main case; Networks & Operating Systems devotes its second half to operating systems, so the relationship covers the networking half only, and it does not cover UM's wireless communication, routing algorithms or network security.

Explicitly unmatched: the only UCR course with operating-systems content (Networks & Operating Systems) is already placed against Computer Networks, to which it devotes its first half, and UCR has no separate operating-systems course.

Explicitly unmatched: the catalogue lists this year-3 course with the same description as the year-2 Operating Systems, and the only UCR course with operating-systems content is already placed against Computer Networks.

Both teach relational database systems with SQL, relational theory and query processing; UM's course also covers data modelling and database design in more depth and the internal workings of database systems.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on digital logic, processor architecture or hardware description.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on multithreading, multiprocessing or parallel programming.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on programming embedded systems.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on computer or information security.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on high-performance computing or parallel and distributed systems, and no project module attached to one.
Artificial intelligence, machine learning and robotics

Both introduce intelligent or rational agents that act on their environment and the search and problem-solving methods that let them do so; Introduction to Artificial Intelligence also covers societal and ethical issues of AI, which UCR teaches in AI Ethics.

Both teach image processing and computer vision: UM's module combines an Image and Video Processing course (camera geometry, filtering, segmentation, frequency-domain transforms and deep-learning approaches) with a Human-Computer Interaction project, and Image Processing & Computer Vision matches the course half but not the interaction project.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on human-computer interaction, user-centred interface design or intelligent user interaction.

Both examine philosophical and ethical questions about intelligent machines and computing, including whether machines can think and how ethics relates to computer systems; The History and Philosophy of Computing also traces the historical development of computing technology, which AI Ethics does not.
Research, project work, thesis and open electives
Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course is a semester-long group software project; Project 1-1 is organised as team project work alongside courses.
Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course is a semester-long group software project.
Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course is a software project for external customers.
Explicitly unmatched: this is open elective space for six courses of the department's or the Faculty of Science and Engineering's elective list, and no UCR course corresponds to a specific elective.
Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no bachelor thesis course; the standardized optional independent research element is placed against this component.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of programming, algorithms, mathematics and databases or data. The Maastricht University Computer Science bachelor additionally includes specialist work in computer architecture, operating systems, computer security, parallel and high-performance computing, embedded programming, programming languages and the theory of computing, together with semester-long software projects and a bachelor's thesis. UCR students can instead combine its computer-science, mathematics, data-science and artificial-intelligence courses, but those specialist components are not offered at the same level of depth.

The Maastricht University Computer Science bachelor includes a more extensive sequence in programming, software engineering and computer systems. At UCR, students can study software development, algorithms, databases, networks and operating systems, but UCR does not offer the same depth or sequence in computer science.
